utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll begin by giving the Chamber's oral ruling on the preparation and presentation of the Defence case. There is then a matter I want to deal with briefly in private session for a short period. Turning to the oral ruling, a written order will be available today and is authoritative. The Trial Chamber has had to balance the need for the accused to have adequate time for the preparation of his case and the need for an expeditious trial. In this connection, the Trial Chamber has taken into consideration that the accused has the support of two legal associates. It is apparent from his cross-examination that he has been provided with detailed information. The Trial Chamber has also taken into consideration the fact that the trial has already taken 19 months. The accused has been in detention for two years and three months, during which time he's had the opportunity to consider and make preparations for his Defence. The Trial Chamber notes that the accused has elected to represent himself. While this cannot be allowed to give him an advantage, the Tribunal should provide appropriate logistical assistance to enable the accused to prepare his defence whilst in detention. It is with these matters in mind that the Trial Chamber now gives its ruling concerning the preparation and presentation of the Defence case. Preparation for the Defence case. The trial will be adjourned for three months between the close of the Prosecution case and the commencement of the Defence case to facilitate the accused in the preparation of his case. This adjournment will be subject to any hearing which the Trial Chamber may order. The accused, within six weeks of the close of the Prosecution case, shall file the following documents: The list of witnesses he intends to call, including the name of each witness, a summary of the facts on which each witness will testify, and an indication of whether the witness will testify in person or, pursuant to Rule 92 bis, by way of written statement or use of a transcript of testimony from other proceedings before the Tribunal. He shall also file the list of exhibits he intends to offer in his case and is obliged to serve on the Prosecutor copies of the exhibits so listed. The Trial Chamber will thereafter hold a Pre-Defence Conference for the following purposes: To review the accused's witness list and set the number of witnesses he'll be entitled to call; to determine the time which will be available to the accused to present his case; and to deal with such other matters as the Chamber considers appropriate for the purposes of facilitating the presentation of the accused's case, including practical arrangements to be made to bring Defence witnesses to the Tribunal, and for the accused to prepare for his examination-in-chief. I turn to the presentation of the Defence case. At the commencement of the Defence case, the accused shall be entitled to open his case in respect of all three indictments against him subject to a time limit to be imposed by the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber may refuse to hear a witness whose name does not appear on the accused's list of witnesses. If the accused wishes to add any witnesses or exhibits to his witness list after the Pre-Defence Conference, he must apply to the Chamber for permission to do so, showing good cause. In the examination by the accused of his witnesses, he should bear in mind at all times that the Trial Chamber exercises control over the mode and order of interrogating witnesses and presenting evidence so as to assure it is effective for the ascertainment of truth and to avoid the needless consumption of time. The accused is reminded that his time will be limited and that he should focus on relevant areas of evidence. The accused is encouraged to avail himself of the provisions under Rule 92 bis with respect to the admission of evidence in written form. If he so desires, the accused may appear as a witness in his own defence. In this respect, he is reminded of annex A to the Chamber's order of the 19th of February, 2002 concerning his right of silence, the relevant parts of which will be attached to the written decision confirming these orders. I finish by dealing with practical arrangements for the preparation and presentation of the Defence case. The Registrar is hereby ordered to provide the accused with facilities in a privileged setting to confer with witnesses and others relevant to his defence, facilities in a privileged setting to review and work with documents and other material relevant to his defence, logistical support with regard to witnesses and facilities to prepare for the presentation of his case. That, as I say, is the order of the Trial Chamber, which will be in written form. There is a matter I wish to deal with now in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Bauer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: The Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to say that I categorically protest against this ruling of yours because it does not enable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No, this -- it wasn't a matter for debate or an invitation to argument. This was a ruling. Now, that is the ruling which we have made. Now, let us get on with the witnesses. If you would call the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every decision or ruling can be re-examined and abolished, and that is my request and demand, that it be rethought and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've just given it. We're not going to abolish it, as you call it, now. We've just given it. If there comes a time when some matter has to be considered, we'll consider it, but that certainly Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. hasn't arisen at the moment. Yes, Ms. Bauer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution is ready to call protective witness C-1160, pursuant to Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Witness, by a court order, you have been granted the protective measures of facial distortion and have been assigned a pseudonym throughout the proceedings. You will be known as Witness C-1160 throughout your testimony. The usher will show you now a piece of paper, and if you could confirm just with a simple yes or no answer whether this is your name and your personal details.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness C-1160, did you have the opportunity to review a statement that you gave to an ICTY investigator over the course of the last few days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: And did you have the opportunity, in the presence of a representative of the court, to sign a declaration affirming the statement's accuracy and truthfulness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would offer this statement into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the pseudonym sheet is 541 under seal, and the statement is 542.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I'll commence with the summary. The witness is of Croat ethnicity and was 32 years of age at the time of the events. He was a resident of Novi Sad in the Vojvodina and conducted business throughout the region of Eastern Slavonia and Vojvodina. On 5th November 1991, the witness was arrested in Titov Vrabas, which is in Vojvodina, for no apparent reasons, other than driving a car with Croatian license plates. He was taken to the police station for interrogation. Subsequently he was transferred to the Novi Sad police station, where the interrogation continued. The witness was shocked by the amount of detailed background that the police had obviously gathered on him, including on his family and his exact movements over a substantial period of time. The witness was never informed about any allegations against him, nor were his rights ever read to him. After two full days of questioning, the police in civilian clothes took him to the Paragovo barracks in the Fruska Gora area. And for Your Honours' information, most of the locations are on a map in the map binder, Exhibit 326, tab 8, which was tendered with -- through Witness C-037. It's not in the Croatian atlas, I'm afraid; it is a separate map that was tendered. In the Paragovo barracks, he was received by a military policeman who routinely took his belongings and personal details.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: He was imprisoned in a tiny cell, which he shared with another eight to nine Croat detainees. Two JNA officers interrogated the witness the following day, again not giving him any reason for the arrest or detention. Afterwards, he was driven to another JNA headquarters, which he couldn't recognise at that time. The military policemen looked inside the van, he was capped, and discussed how they would slaughter him. As soon as the van drove off, the witness was terrified and thought they would kill him. Shortly after that, the witness arrived at an agricultural complex in the village of Begejci. There another JNA military policeman received him and said that he had arrived at Logor camp. The same man threw the witness against a barbed wire fence and beat him until he was bloodied all over. The witness later heard that many guards at the camp, including this individual, had a criminal background and that they had been released at the outbreak of the war to serve the military police. When the witness entered the stables of this agricultural complex, he saw what he at first thought was cabbage covered with blankets. He found out that there were about 240 men and 20 women lying on the concrete floor. The witness recognised some of the men being from different parts of Eastern Slavonia. The prisoners were only allowed to stand when they were taken outside to sing the national -- Yugoslav national anthem or during meals. Prisoners were provided with little food and it was of very poor quality. The hygienic conditions were dreadful and soon the camp suffered an outbreak of lice. Reflectors inside the stables were switched on throughout the night, making it impossible to sleep. A certain JNA colonel or lieutenant colonel, Zivanovic, was in charge of the camp and came to see the detainees on two occasions. Every night a group of drunk military policemen would come to the stable and inflict on the detainees different forms of humiliation, including severe beatings. For instance, each prisoner had to say his prison number, and after which he would receive a baton blow on the head. On some nights, prisoners were forced to run over the bare bodies of other prisoners. Once the detainees had to participate in a mock execution, allegedly as revenge for a killed officer. For more than half an hour they were lined up against a wall and feared being shot any minute. A 60-year-old prisoner died following a particular severe beating. There was never any inquiry into the circumstances of his death. The witness was called on several occasions for interrogations. The patterns used were always the same: There was a JNA officer asking questions with three or four military policemen standing guard. After each question and answer, the witness was punched by the military policemen, no matter what he answered. At one point the military policemen pretended to shoot the witness. After they had sufficiently intimidated the witness, the interrogation continued. Again, the witness was never told any reason for his detention nor what he was accused of. He also did not see any judge or a lawyer during the whole time in his detention. After about 20 days in detention, the ICRC came to register the prisoners and undertook to inform families. The military police guards in the camp hid ten prisoners during that time from the ICRC. Shortly after, the witness received a visit from his wife and daughter. A television team, whose cameraman was in a JNA uniform, filmed the day of the visit. Before the witness, however, met his visitors, he was beaten all the way up to the point and humiliated. On 10 December 1991, the witness was released after five weeks of detention in a town in Bosanski Samac. Approximately 630 mostly Croat prisoners from various detention camps were exchanged for around 129 Serb JNA officers. Only then did the witness find out that the alleged reason for his detention was that he was accused of being the main HDZ organiser in the Vojvodina, although he had never any involvement with the party movement. Furthermore, he learned that his family had made inquiries about his whereabouts immediately after he had disappeared. The authorities had lied and informed them that he had been released immediately. That concludes the summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 1160, up until November 1989, you had lived in Zagreb, when you got married with a lady from Novi Sad and you moved to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. live in Novi Sad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that in -- just before the war, you worked as a representative of a company and in that capacity you covered the area of Eastern Slavonia and the northern part of Serbia, or actually the whole of Vojvodina, as a kind of commercial representative; is that right? What company was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Mladinska Knjiga.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: In 1989 I tried to do that work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you actually covered this part of Eastern Slavonia, an area where the conflicts started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: At that time, there were no such indications. The situation had not started to worsen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did it start to worsen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: When I could no longer cover that area. This occurred towards the end of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you say that it became much more difficult to travel and do your job. You say this on page 2, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Serbs were crossing from Eastern Slavonia into Vojvodina, and of course then I could no longer be active in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why were Serbs crossing from Eastern Slavonia to Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Allegedly conflicts were worsening after Borovo Naselje and they were being expelled. That is what was said. But I also learnt some other things; that is, they didn't see anyone. People were simply awakened during the night and transported by buses across, and I learnt this talking to people as I was travelling around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what you are saying that happened, that is, when Serbs were fleeing Eastern Slavonia, you say they did that without any cause.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I can't claim anything because I didn't see anything happening. I'm just telling you what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In paragraph 5, page 2, you say that you then started to train a younger man, a Serb, to work with you. As far as I understand it, you needed him to be able to travel more easily; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I'm talking about this year, that when I was working and travelling, they would ask me where I came from and what I was, and problems had started so I felt that the circumstances were no longer regular.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that is why you hired that man.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Not just for that reason. I needed several people. But in any case, it would be easier for me. The new area that I was supposed to cover, I had my own marketing agency which mediated between the manufacturer of cosmetics and the consumers, and they requested several people. But when a new area was being covered, after the experiences I had had, I no longer dared travel alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You yourself say that your work required that you hire several men.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I just said. That is why I didn't dare go alone, because I had already experienced some unpleasantness in certain places, not everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us the name of this man?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this reveals the identity of the witness, he can tell us in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, to be on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand it, that man was with you when, at the beginning of November, as you say - it was probably the 5th of November, 1991 - when you were taken into custody to the Secretariat of the Interior in Vrbas; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Where exactly were you taken in in Vrbas? Do you know in what part of town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I don't know, but I was taken to the SUP. I was sitting in my car until he went inside to arrange a meeting so that we could start working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I heard a moment ago from the summary read by Ms. Pack [sic] that the only reason that you were taken into custody was that you had Croatian license plates. Is that right? Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: No. I don't know the reason to this day. One of the assumptions was that it was because I was in a car with Croatian license plates. Of course, there were others in the same situation, and until then I had had no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But when you were taken into custody, as we heard from the summary, you were shocked to -- by the details they knew about you and your movement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Just then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see, just then. So I assume the only reason could not have been your license plates, but surely this information they had and -- that shocked you, because they knew what you had been doing and where you moved.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I wasn't shocked when I was taken in. But after the interview and interrogation, after I went to the camp itself, that is what I had in mind. I referred to the interrogation, which went on for two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you referred to the date of the 5th of November, 1991, was that the time when there was fighting around Vukovar and many other places in Eastern Slavonia and in Western Slavonia also?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: At that time, according to my knowledge, there was a conflict in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know how far Vrbas is from the border with Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: About 50-odd kilometres, roughly. I haven't been there for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And on the second page, in paragraph 6, you stated that they didn't treat you badly at that time, they questioned you about what you were doing, what your work was, where you travelled, and things like that. Is that right? I didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I said yes, that was true. What does it mean to treat me badly? I was probably exposed to regular procedure. By the end of the interrogation, I noticed changes; I wouldn't be given bread or water or anything, and this went on all day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by "all day," when you say five hours later you were driven to Novi Sad? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I'm talking about Novi Sad, about the provincial SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you were interrogated there too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes. After Vrbas, which lasted so many hours, I was transported -- both of us, actually, were transported in this vehicle. The co-driver turned round to face us and the driver. Both of them were wearing police uniforms. And the one -- the co-driver was facing us with a pistol, and my car was being driven by a third policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Look at what you said on page 3, paragraph 1. You say that "I had the impression that they thought I was a spy because of the way that I travelled about." Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Which paragraph? Which number paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 3, first paragraph. Page 1 is numbered "2," so I don't want you to be confused by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: If it is of assistance, it's paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because of my travelling around, not because of the way I travelled around. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just have your statement in English. I wasn't given it in Serbo-Croatian. And you say, "I got the impression that they thought that I was a spy because of the way that I travelled about."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, what is the -- what's the question, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you engage in collecting information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But give me, please, a precise answer. Did they consider you to be a spy or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: That was what I thought. I just said what I thought at the time, because there was no reason for all this to happen to me. I couldn't see any reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you drew the conclusion that you had been arrested because they considered you to be a spy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I thought that that was probably the reason for questioning me, because the way in which they questioned me, the details they went into, endeavouring to draw information from me that I didn't have, that is why I said that, because that was my conclusion, that I thought -- that they thought I was a spy

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: May I infer from that you don't believe that you were arrested because you were a Croat working there but because they suspected that you collected intelligence, in view of the fact that you moved around in your work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I still think because -- that I was arrested because I was a Croat, because the colleague who worked with me and who was a Serb was released immediately; whereas, having met people who went through similar treatment as I did, I gathered that quite a number of Croats were rounded up mostly without cause. So there is every indication to believe that it was because I was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, in view of the fact that you lived in Novi Sad, how many Croats, how many thousands of Croats were living and working not just in Novi Sad but all over Vojvodina, without any one of them being in any special situation because he was a Croat? Why would you be in such a special situation if it was not because they suspected you of being a spy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I knew very few Croats, nor did I have many business friends of that ethnicity. There were more of other ethnicities. So I don't know how the others were treated, other Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. On page 3, paragraph 2, you said that you were questioned in Novi Sad until about 2.00 in the morning and that then you were taken home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then they returned your car to you and you went home. Was that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: No. It wasn't like that. I was questioned until late into the night. I was driven home with an order. They told me that I had come back -- that I had to come back by 10.00, I think it was, the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you weren't arrested, since they drove you back home and told you to come back again by 10.00 in the morning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: If I had spent the whole day in the police station, how can I say that I wasn't arrested?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they just talked to you over there and then let you go home and told you to come back on your own. Nobody was taking you under any kind of coercion, but they were just telling you to come back in the morning, as you yourself say. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't know why I was released and my documents kept there. I had to go back. This may have been part of this whole examination, to see what I would do or -- how do I know what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where did they talk to you in Novi Sad? In which building? In which state institution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I think it was the provincial SUP. I don't really remember the building any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that morning in Novi Sad you were interviewed by a man whose name you don't know; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I don't know the name of any one of the investigators from Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that he was very well informed about where you -- the place of your birth in Croatia. I won't read it out because it's a small place and it could perhaps call in question your status of a protected witness. So he was extremely well-known, as you say -- well informed about your home town, that he knew everything about your movements there a week before, where you had gone before these events; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 3 of your statement, paragraph 4, you say that "The JNA had withdrawn from the barracks," which is about 10 kilometres from your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: It handed -- it surrendered its weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It surrendered weapons because it was blocked by the National Guards Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I don't know, I wasn't there, but what I just said I heard from others. And this was visible afterwards too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this could be seen afterwards.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: It was possible to move around in the area where the barracks used to be. Two days later I went to Novi Sad and I passed by there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say, [In English] "Which is 10 kilometres from --" [Interpretation] 10 kilometres from your home town. And then you say, [In English] "A gunfire. It was not a significant battle," [Interpretation] Then you say, [In English] "There were no deaths that I know of and the garrison was not small, because we were close to the Hungarian border. I was told by whoever was organising things there to make up a guard duty on one of the streets. It was a local arrangement." [Interpretation] All right. So in your town, where you say there had been some gunfire but minor gunfire, and you say it was not a significant battle, so only a week prior to your arrest somebody who had organised things there said that you should take up guard duty on one of the streets; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I had come from Zagreb. I came back in the morning, around 6.00, and I was asked to come to a meeting. And then I found out what was going on. We stood in front of the building for an entire day, all of that day. Of course, I was unarmed, I didn't have any weapons. And everything I mentioned is what I heard. It's not that I moved anywhere from the centre of town. This meant that defence of the town had been organised in this way. However, since I did not live there, in my home town, of course my friends did not really have much confidence in me. They didn't know what I thought and so on and so forth, so I was in a situation which required that I behave - I don't know - in some way that should have been -- whatever. This statement that had to do with the barracks, that's the only Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. thing I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But as far as I can see, you were told to take up some kind of guard duty; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: We were assigned to various streets, wearing civilian clothes, and that day, if - I don't know - the army would get out of barracks and move towards Osijek and in this way attack the town -- well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that you yourself were not armed at that point in time, whereas some of the local men had some light weaponry; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Light weaponry in the sense of hunting guns and pistols. That's what I saw. The barrels that they referred to -- that's what they were saying. I'm just saying what I saw there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also say -- well, you do not say that anybody made weapons of their own. You say I was not armed [In English] "although some of the locals had light weapons." [Interpretation] And when did you return to your family in Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Two days later. So the second day in the afternoon, that's when I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So all of this in your home town lasted for less than two days.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that was going on at the time when JNA soldiers were attacked in the vicinity of your town -- or rather, in your town and around your town; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I happened to be there at the moment when this was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since you happened to be there at the moment when this was taking place, as you put it yourself, you say that you took part in guard duty, although you were unarmed. Did you take part in the fighting, Mr. C-1160?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I did not take part in any kind of fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were just a person who was present at the time when this was happening.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were on some kind of guard duty, though you were unarmed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I was unarmed, whereas the man who was with me had a pistol, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the name of the man who told you to take up guard duty and the man who was with you and who was armed? If you don't want to say this in open session, perhaps we could move into private session.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I can say it in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In view of your participation or, as you say, presence and partial participation in these developments, you were actually a temporary member of the National Guards Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: In case anything bad happened in my home town, of course I would have taken part, and it just so happened that I was in such a situation that I had to defend my home town in a way. According to the information that they gave me then, and all the things that could happen - my parents are there, my relatives, et cetera - I don't know how else I should have behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm just establishing the facts here. However, you claim that the man who interrogated you knew everything about you, even what you wore during that fighting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I said that, that he knew where I had been when all of those things were taking place during that day or two that is being referred to. He knew that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that at the time you wore a ZNG uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I had not worn a uniform since 1988, which was the last time when I went to do some shooting -- training as a JNA reservist, when I was called up. Since then, I had not worn a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the man who spoke to you knew everything about what you did in your home town. I'm not going to mention the name. And he arrested you practically for nothing. That is what you say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: He knew the names of persons. He asked me about the names and the positions held by various people in the town. And of course, I didn't know what positions they held. I told him what happened a while before that, but I said that I was there for a very short period of time, and nobody really confided in me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it clear that nobody had arrested you because you were a Croat, because otherwise they would have arrested thousands of other Croats who then and all those years lived in Serbia, including Novi Sad, where you lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, I'd put it in a different way. If there was so much information about me, then also they could have known that I had not done a thing that would have caused me to be arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 6, also on page 3, you say that they treated you correctly, because they explained that they knew that your father-in-law was a retired JNA captain. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They also questioned you about the Ustashas, who had committed atrocities against women and children in Eastern Slavonia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, the questions were the same, like those put to the other detainees. So it was my understanding that this was probably a system that had already been in place. I was asked because -- I mean, I was asked whether I knew about this man who wore a necklace made of children's fingers and also whether I knew about an Ustasha killing a baby in a cradle and putting dynamite or a shell into the baby's stomach. That's the kind of questions that were addressed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know anything about these events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Of course I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about these things now, about the atrocities that were committed then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I don't know about that even now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph on page 3, you say that they did not believe that you were innocent and that they tried to intimidate you by saying that they would send you to defend Serb houses in Papuk; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: That's what they were telling me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Serb houses in Papuk had been attacked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: That's what I heard from the interrogators, from the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who attacked these houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: It was always presented in the same way, Ustashas, like previously. It was the Ustashas who attacked Serb houses in Papuk too. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. That's the way they put it. I heard all of this from the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that this was a place near the front line where it was believed that the Ustashas were killing Serbs. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I stated that this was at the front line, where the investigators believed, what I had said previously, that the Ustashas were attacking and killing Serbs. These are the words of the investigators. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But the town that you went to, was that on the front line actually?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I was told that the Ustashas were attacking Serb houses in Papuk, and I consider then that to be fighting, a front line. That's my interpretation. And where the front line actually was, I really do not know. As I said, I did not even know that this had been going on before I heard about it from the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Your participation in these activities of the National Guards Corps boils down to those two days only.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: It wasn't the National Guards Corps. It was the defence of the town itself. So there were no uniforms. These were men in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. After the interrogation in Novi Sad, they took you in an unknown direction, you say, to a military facility that you did not know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I was never there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you say where it is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, I know where I was -- I mean, later on I found out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you said. Where was it that you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: A military facility near the -- I mean, after the provincial SUP. It's a military facility called Paragovo. I heard about that only later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where is this military facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I was driven during the night, so Fruska Gora -- Paragovo-Fruska Gora. That's what they said to me. I did not check this. I did not look it up on a map or anything, so I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You thought they were taking you to Papuk, and that is why you were very frightened; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Since the last threat before they took me away was that that's where they would take me, what else could I have thought?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say in your statement that they told you that they would take you to Papuk to defend Serb houses. Here in this summary that was read by Ms. Pack [sic] you say -- I do apologise. On the other side there are so many persons that are involved that I cannot remember all the names, Mr. May. They change so frequently. So Ms. Bauer read, if I heard this correctly, that they were taking you to kill you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I cannot describe all the things that go through a person's mind at moments like those, so everything I said was true. All of this was after the things I had experienced, so what else could I have thought?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If they told you that they were taking you to Papuk to defend the Serb houses there, and if that was a threat that they were addressing, so on the basis of what do you say that they threatened you that they would take you out and kill you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Is it sufficient to say that they would push me unarmed in front of troops? That is not something that is unheard of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They told you that they would take you to defend Serb houses. They did not say that they would take you out to kill you. Now, what you thought in your very own head, that they would take you out and kill you, that is not something that they said to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: What they said to me, that they would take me to defend Serb houses, that is one of the sentences that they uttered, not to mention cannon fodder and other words they referred to. So this one sentence is not the only thing that said in -- it was not the only thing that led me to believe what I had thought at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1160, I am not going into that, what you could have thought at the time or what you thought at the time. I just want to establish that not at a single point in time did they tell you that they were taking you out to kill you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: The way in which they did all of this could not have led me to believe anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they never said to you or threatened you that they were -- would take you out to kill you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: What you are saying now was during the period of questioning in Novi Sad, at the provincial SUP there. What followed were things that could not have been put in that way, and I explained this gradually, how things developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. They took you to this military facility, and then they questioned you there as well. You say that you were questioned by a major and a captain; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: At that moment, I can -- at this moment, rather, I can say that I do not know what the ranks were. One of them was a captain for sure; I know that. There were NCOs among them as well. There were different people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they also had information about you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. I wrote the statement in the provincial SUP and the statement accompanied me wherever I went. And of course they had all this information available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that the major put a series of questions of a military nature, and you say that he asked you about your own observations during your travels around Vojvodina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: For the most part, he asked me about arms. And actually, he wanted to see what I knew about weapons and other things, of course. It was one and the same thing that was asked about all the time. And later on they were probably trying to compare all these different statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And so there you wrote the statements in your own hand, just as you had done in Novi Sad, right, where you were also questioned and interrogated.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I wrote the statements myself, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say you wrote out the statement covering five pages. What were those five pages about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I wrote about everything, from my education and everything else. You could take 55 pages to write down your own history if you have a little imagination or if you have a talent for writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, without going into the details and talent for writing, which I'm sure you possess, let me ask you whether in those five pages, did you write anything about answers to questions that were asked you and matters relating to what you yourself call a series -- a lot of military-type questions, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't give them an answer because I knew nothing about any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine, Mr. 1166 [as interpreted]. As far as I was able to gather from this statement of yours, you're a musician too, aren't you, alongside the job you also hold?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, for just one period, that period of time, I wasn't a musician nor did I earn money by playing music. During that time and also after the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you said that you played in a well-known Zagreb band. Now, I don't want to ask about that, but what I do want to establish is what you said. You mentioned a major and a captain having questioned you and they even knew about that, about you being a member of the band. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, I didn't play music during that period of time. They were just some guys playing at a party. That's what the captain told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he told you about that, did he, that you were a musician?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: No, that they played music in front of some military facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they knew everything about you, and yet you say they arrested you for no reason.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Let me repeat: In view of the fact that they knew everything Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. about me, then they could have also known that I had done nothing to warrant my being arrested and ending up in a concentration camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you were in a cell with another -- or with some other Croats, or rather, with one Croat. That's what you say. And he was the owner of some cafe in Zagreb; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I said I recognised a man who happened to be the owner of this cafe in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why had he been arrested? Did you learn of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, we couldn't talk amongst ourselves very much. I just learnt that he had -- drove a car there and he was arrested in Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you say there were two other men from some village in Vojvodina who took place -- took part in rallies held against -- to protest against the mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, these were all talks -- we had short conversations and chats, and that's what these people said. Now, they said that they had attended a rally to protest against the mobilisation, and when they were dispersing - that's what they told me, at least - that when they were dispersing and going home, they were all rounded up and brought there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you remember their names, then, and the place they came from in Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know the place or their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: No, I don't. I've forgotten. I don't know their names or the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, at around 2300 hours of that same day, you were taken for interrogation once again, on a second occasion, and the major and the captain, as you claim on page 6, paragraph 2, they just interrogated you briefly, about half an hour; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, I was handing over that statement -- making the statement. That's why it lasted such a brief time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm interested in the interview -- in the conversation. You say it lasted half an hour. What did you talk to them about on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: About the statement I had written.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what did you discuss.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, he analysed my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any specific parts that you analysed from the statement, any portions of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on that occasion, nobody beat you or mistreated you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Not then, unless you consider mistreatment the fact that I was incarcerated in a cell. I did receive one blow at Paragovo when we were cleaning in front of the -- sweeping in front of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking you about during the interview.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: No, nothing happened during the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you said that the captain was rough with you verbally, in his verbal address to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, that took -- that happened several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, he would be nice to start off with and then would turn ugly and so on. One man would be nice and the other man would be brutal or, rather, one would be well disposed towards you and the other would be rough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that the next day you were transferred to Begejci, a place near Zrenjanin, the town of Zrenjanin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I was driven off in the morning, and I think I say this in my statement, but let me repeat that, while I was being taken out of the building in Paragovo, I was told that as I was carrying something for breakfast, that I couldn't go back to have breakfast. So that was the last thing I heard. So once again, psychological pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, when they said that you didn't need breakfast - that's what you said, I think - that you understood that you were being taken off to be killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, I was driven off alone in a Black Maria with -- I think that's what the van is called, with small windows, and I was taken off by the warrant officer and four others, other policemen wearing the white belts, police belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, these policemen with the white police belts, was their conduct correct and proper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, if you -- if we take it that their shoving us in and pushing us around was direct and proper, then I suppose they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. You now see that -- you say that the first time you were beaten was by a man called Zare and you said that that happened when you got to Begejci; is that right? What happened? Was it a centre for war prisoners or what in Begejci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: When the door opened, he made me bow my head and put my hands behind my back. So what could I have seen like that? He just told me that it wasn't a hotel and I don't know what else. What can I call it? Well, it turned out to be a concentration camp, in fact. And at that point in time he began beating me. He shoved me head into the wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you say that this military policeman, that actually he was a criminal who had been released from prison before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: During the time I spent in that camp, one of the people who would come in - and there were five or six of them who came in - he was drunk, and he said he couldn't care less whether he was behind bars or behind a wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So on the basis of that, you concluded that criminals had been released from prison to become military policemen; is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, that might have been the case -- it might have been translated that way, but I do consider that they were criminals nonetheless. And what I said is that this was linked up. It was my assumption. I assumed that they had been doing prison sentences in prison and then had been trained as military policemen and reservists and transferred and that they were in fact serving their prison sentence by being these military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So according to what Ms. Bauer read out, it is your assumption that they were criminals who had become military policemen; is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, this man Zare, who beat me, was a policeman and he had scars on his face. I don't know how else to describe it. That's how I experienced the whole thing, anyway. Those were my impressions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we can meet -- we come across various people with tattoos on them and they're not considered to be criminals. You said he had tattoos.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, he was a criminal, as far as I was concerned, judging by his conduct. It wasn't the first time he had behaved that way, or the last, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we can't know that, so let's not enter into those details. But that -- those were your conclusions and observations, but you had no actual information that somebody had turned criminals into military policemen, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: All I can say is this: I wrote my statement on the basis of my own experience and how I experienced that particular situation, so I don't have any confidential inside information of any kind, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, you don't have any information. But you remember another military policeman nicknamed Rambo; is that what you claim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information and knowledge about this man, Rambo, that he had a criminal record or anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I think that that's what Rambo himself said on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You think he told you that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who said this, but I think one of them said that they couldn't care less whether they were behind bars or behind wires, it was the same thing to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was on the basis of that statement that you drew your conclusions. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, yes. But a long time has gone by since then for me to be able to remember all the details. I just said what I remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, very well. But according to what you yourself say in Begejci, you were mostly beaten by an Albanian by the name of Krasniqi and a Croat called Mirko, but you don't know his last name, last name unknown; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I didn't know Mirko's surname, but I didn't say that they were the ones who beat me most. They did beat me, yes, amongst others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this Albanian Krasniqi and this Mirko from Croatia, he was from Biljani Osijek [phoen]; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And they were at the entrance to the shed or stable and they were standing between the military policemen and us. So if anybody had to go to the toilet or anything, they had to pass by these men. And one of them always had to be awake. And if any new detainees were brought in, both of them had to be there, and they were standing up, whereas we were lying down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you recognised a certain man called Milas from Opatovci in Eastern Slavonia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Stjepan Milas. He had a shop. And when I worked with cosmetics, he would purchase some cosmetics from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, just like this other man, Kruno Farkas, whom you mention, were they members of the Croatian National Guards Corps? They were, weren't they, Mr. 1160?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I learnt that Kruno was a member and that he was in Ilok at one point in time, but he was captured wearing civilian clothing leaving Ilok. As for Stjepan Milas, I think he was some functionary in his home town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right, then, but were the people who were arrested actually people who had fought within the ranks of the Croatian National Guard Corps? Amongst them -- by mistake they ranked you amongst them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Of the 500 odd people at the end, some 20 -- approximately 20 people, I don't know the exact number, from the surroundings of Bileca, were in uniform of the Croatian National Guards. All the others were wearing civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you say of this man Farkas, that he was indeed a member of the Croatian National Guards Corps but that he withdrew wearing civilian clothing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: He was in that place, but I assume he was dressed like that, and I deduced this from what he said later on, in my conversation with him later on. He was organised in the defence of his town or village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 8, paragraph 9, you claim that one day, as you yourself say, two black men were brought in, but you don't know where they were from nor did you know their names. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I didn't know the names, but according to the rumours that went round in the camp, they were students from Sri Lanka who studied in Skopje somewhere. They were students in Skopje but had come to Belgrade to fetch some documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand it, they were some sort of foreign mercenaries; right? They were foreign mercenaries; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, when the military policemen came to that -- the stable, they would say that two mercenaries -- two Croatian mercenaries had arrived, which means on the one hand we have this piece of information and, on the other, that other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the commander of the Croatian Guards -- National Guards and that group of ZNGs who were in the prison, the commander was a man named Grizbauer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Grizbaum or Grizbauer, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what unit of the ZNG was it? Do you know? What ZNG unit was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I don't know what unit, what the unit's name was. All I do know is that they were from around Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know what part of the front they were captured on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: They said that they had taken part on an attack on a border hut somewhere and that they were surrounded and captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they attacked a military border hut, is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes, that's what was said, that they had gone into action, into operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they said that somebody had betrayed them and that when they arrived they were surrounded -- found themselves surrounded and captured.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes. How else would I know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you should have in mind you have five minutes left now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I understood it, Mr. May, that I began after half past 9.00. But I am sure you have more precise evidence. But I'll hurry along.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that was the battlefront that they were captured on, and an ambush -- you say they were betrayed, that nobody shot at them, that they were captured during an ambush and arrested; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes. I'm saying what I remember them having told me or having heard about the incident. Dogs were used to hunt them down, and one of the men was bitten by one of the dogs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the frontier guards always have dogs with them. That's common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, although you refer to this as a concentration camp, the prison in which the members of the National Guards Corps were incarcerated, that you nonetheless had medical care there, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: All I saw was a lady passing by wearing civilian clothes but a white coat over her clothes. She wasn't from the army. That's what I say. But later on there was a doctor in camp that was there with us, and I assume they knew who he was. But that medical care was very scant. All it meant was the bandaging of wounds, like that man who had been bitten by the guard dogs, and perhaps some tranquilisers were handed around. That's all, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you wrote to your wife from Begejci and she in fact visited you with your daughter. She came to Begejci to visit you with your daughter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, yes, when the Red Cross came. So the Red Cross wrote the letter, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But she visited you, together with a cousin - I don't want to read her name out - and she tried to intervene with the warden, prison warden; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, because they didn't know why I was being held there in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say she was upset after talking to the warden. Did she tell you why she was upset?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Not then, but several months later when we were in Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did she say why she had been so upset?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: She told me that she had learnt that I was the main organiser for the HDZ party in Vojvodina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that was what they believed. But you were exchanged on the 10th of December, 1991 in Bosanski Samac; isn't that right, Mr. 1160?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So how long did you spend in prison altogether and in the -- with the ZNG group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I didn't hear the first part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How long did you spend in prison altogether with that group of ZNG members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: It was a small group of about 20. I was there with some 500 civilians from Vukovar and the other places in Eastern Slavonia. Now, you keep insisting upon this group of ZNG members. I don't think it was a very important group of people or a large one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you were -- an indictment was never raised against you in Yugoslavia, nor were you found guilty of anything. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: No, I don't remember, except for traffic misdemeanours, traffic offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did you last stay in Yugoslavia, actually? When were you last there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: What did you say? When was I in ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When were you in Yugoslavia last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: In Yugoslavia. I see. Well, Yugoslavia, it's not called that any more, is it? So I don't know which Yugoslavia you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this: After the war, did you continue to live in Novi Sad or did you go elsewhere? Did you stay with your wife, who is a native of Novi Sad, to live in Novi Sad or did you go anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: To Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't return to the area after that, did you, at any time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I was there recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Recently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes, recently, on business.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you there after 1991 -- or rather, when were you there first after 1991, after the events we discussed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I was in Pozarevac with some people -- with a band, playing with a band.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Three years ago, three and a half years ago. I'm not quite sure. We were invited by the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To play on the radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: No. We were called by Radio Pozarevac to play there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Well, I said; three years ago roughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic or Mr. Kay, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if some copying is done, it will be much quicker for this witness after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know what the copying is, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I have it here, but mine has been written on by me and it's probably better to have clean copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn for twenty minutes. Witness C-1160, we're just going to adjourn for 20 minutes. Could you remember not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution. Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, during the break, a copy of a -- an additional statement was provided for Your Honours and the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like you to look at the statement which is going to be produced for you. Have you got it in your hand? Can you see it's a statement in your name? Don't mention your name. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us, first of all, when you made that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I made that statement after the exchange, maybe some ten days after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And who did you make that statement to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I made that statement in my place of birth to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want you to look at some of the details of this statement. First of all, in the first paragraph you can see that it states you were arrested by the police in Vojvodina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Two policemen were in civilian clothes who approached the car. Policemen or milicija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that particular place, I think you've told us, is Titov Vrbas. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And when you refer to a provisional SUP, is it the SUP in Titov Vrbas where you were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I'm referring to the provincial SUP of Novi Sad. That's how it was called. That was the full name of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When we look at this statement, it says that you were taken to the provincial SUP.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: From the SUP in Titov Vrbas, I was driven by car, as I have said, two of us, and then two men in civilian clothes, the driver and the co-driver with the pistol, and a third man in uniform was driving my car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When we've looked at your statement that was produced before the court, we can see on page 2 of it, at paragraph 10 that when you were taken home, you were ordered to return at 7.00 in the following morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is your evidence, then, that they left you alone with your family for that period of time at your home and that you returned voluntarily to the SUP some hours later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: All my things stayed behind in the SUP, my documents, the documents of my firm, my personal documents, and the car with advertising products, samples. So I couldn't do but go back. There was no other thing I could do but go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the statement before the court, it says in paragraph 7 that you were in that station, meaning the police station, and then you were driven to the SUP office in Novi Sad. That indicates that you were at two separate police stations, doesn't it, before you were transferred to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we look at that other statement that I've put before you just a moment ago, at line 14 it says in that statement that you went from the provincial SUP to Paragovo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In that statement, there's no mention of you being in the police station at Novi Sad at all.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I made a distinction. In Titov Vrbas the police station -- the SUP, I was taken there, and then the other one I called the provincial SUP, the one in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In that statement, then, you refer to the provincial SUP but you don't refer to the police station at Titov Vrbas.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: That statement was made -- I was just recounting the events as I knew them. It was a statement -- it was no special statement. Maybe I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm asking you about this other statement that wasn't exhibited before the court, and in that statement it doesn't make a distinction between a police station at Titov Vrbas nor a police station at Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I didn't sign this statement, so I didn't read it. The man was writing it while I was talking, and that is probably why that is not indicated. But I'm sure that I said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The man who took the statement, what was his job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: He was a policeman or an inspector or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was he there to listen to you and write down what you had to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I think that it went as follows: After my return from the camp, it was stated that I should go and make a statement. I reported to a police station, people who were responsible for this, and I made that statement over there. It wasn't an investigator, or at least I didn't see it as being an investigation of any kind. And I don't know whether that man was a professional or whether he was just acting as a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, though, that you knew it was important as to why you were giving a statement about what had happened to you from the 5th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: No. It was my friend who encouraged me to do that, because they Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. knew what had happened to me. No one asked me to come and make that statement. I didn't receive any particular call-up or summons to make that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One other matter: If we look at paragraph 18 of the statement -- the main statement that was exhibited. I appreciate that on the 15th of September you made a correction to the line that says, "To this day I still don't know where they took me."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't find my way. I don't know what exactly you're referring to. The 18th?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 18 of the statement, where you say, "The questioning went on until around 2.00 or 3.00 in the morning."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And then, "They put me in an unmarked car and drove to an army barracks about 30 minutes away. To this day I still don't know where they took me."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: The statement that I made, I think it was three years ago, I didn't prepare myself for it nor did I give detailed thought to things - I thought it would follow a normal course - and just then I couldn't remember the barracks I was taken to. That is why the correction was made now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In that statement that we see that I've produced this morning, it names the place as being Paragovo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you telling the Court that you couldn't remember that place when you made the statement on two dates of interview in June of the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1160
utterances.text: That statement was left like that. I don't remember that we made any corrections. I probably just omitted to do that. And I don't even know whether during those two days I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honours, no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, it won't matter to you whether you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I didn't really want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not for you to say put it in or not, but since there have been questions about it, it may be appropriate to put it in. It may be most convenient, really, if it could be attached to Exhibit 542. There's also an addendum and a sketch plan, and it would seem appropriate if we could attach, Ms. Bauer, I should think, this statement to the -- to the MUP.
