utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We don't have any objections. And if we please could just redact the personal details of the witness for the public version. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes. Witness C-1160, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go, but could you just wait while the blinds are drawn down.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness is the witness Marko Knezic. He does not have any protective measures. And he will actually speak about a region which is on page 37 of the atlas Exhibit 336, the village Slano, north-west of Dubrovnik at the coast, and Bileca, above Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, please state your name.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Marko Knezic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Knezic, you gave a statement to an investigator of the OTP in the year 2000. Did you review and confirm your statement in a proceeding in front of a court officer in June this year?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would like to tender the 92 bis package for this witness. It's the statement, the proceeding, and also the attachment -- attachments to that previous statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 543, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will now read the summary for the witness and just ask a very few questions. Mr. Knezic was 39 years old at the time of the events. He is from the village of Slano, north of Dubrovnik. Slano had a population of 450 to 500 people, mostly Croats. When the events in Vukovar got known and the people in the region felt insecure in the middle of 1991, a crisis committee was formed in Slano. The crisis committee worked in coordination with the local police. The witness participated in the village defence. The village defence had very few weapons, namely hunting rifles. They guarded the communication system, water supply, post office, and the like. On the 3rd of October, 1991, the JNA started shelling Slano and its surroundings. The crisis committee of Slano directed the inhabitants, especially elderly, women, and children, to leave the village. By 4th of October, 1991, only about 30 people remained in Slano.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Knezic, I have just a few questions. This crisis committee in Slano, was it a civilian body or a military body?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: It was a civilian body.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the policemen they cooperated with, were they the regular civilian police or was it special police from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: It was the regular police.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Before the attack, did the population get any warning from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't receive any warning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were the villagers ever requested to surrender their village or to surrender weapons to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: No. I never heard any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the villagers do anything that could have caused the attack of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On the 4th of October, 1991, the JNA attacked Slano with artillery and infantry. The soldiers were wearing SMB uniforms with a red star on the caps. In addition, paramilitary soldiers took part in the attack. The witness, who had not been able to flee when the attack commenced, spent two months in hiding in the rocks above his house, together with his father and a neighbour. From this place where he was hiding, the witness would see JNA and paramilitary soldiers burning the houses and looting them. The father of the witness was captured on the 1st of December, 1991, while the witness, along with his neighbour, surrendered to JNA soldiers from the Uzice Corps on the 4th of December that same year. The witness and his neighbour were mistreated during this surrender. The witness was wounded on his head. On the next day, the 5th of December, the witness was taken to the Bileca prison camp. This prison was first run by the JNA Uzice Corps and later by the JNA Rijeka Corps. The witness was taken to a room, Catacomb, as the prisoners used to call it, and he was chained, together with his neighbour. And a soldier from Uzice came to the room and kicked the witness with his boot and broke his left rib. The next day, the witness was taken to another small room, where he was interrogated by several -- several times by regular JNA officers. He and the other two detainees in that room were hit during -- and beaten during the interrogations. Subsequently, the witness was detained in two different rooms, together with 30 detainees and 50 detainees respectively. Both rooms were overcrowded. The quantity of food in Bileca prison was inadequate. The hygienic conditions were very bad. The prisoners were psychologically and physically mistreated and humiliated in different ways. They were forced to work. On the 23rd of May, 1992, along with 90 to 100 other detainees, the witness was taken to Morinj in Montenegro in JNA buses. The living conditions in Morinj camp regarding food and hygiene were worse than in Bileca. The psychological and physical mistreatment continued. Although beating was a routine, the detainees were particularly beaten on the 13th of June, 1992. On that day two ribs of the witness were broken. Along with 20 other detainees, the witness was exchanged on the 2nd of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Knezic, while you were detained in Bileca or Morinj, were you ever charged with a specific offence or even tried?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I was not charged, and I was not tried.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, this concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Knezic, in paragraph 4 of your statement, you said that you started feeling tensions growing in your region and in your village Slano that you started to organise the defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes. In our village, at that time a Crisis Staff had been organised. I've already said that. People who organised the defence of the village protected various facilities, anything that had to do with the economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, Mr. Knezevic [as interpreted], what were these tensions that were on the rise in your village? What was going on in your village at the time? What led to this rise in tensions?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: We were informed by way of the media about attacks against Vukovar. We saw that something unusual was going on in our homeland, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So that means that you started organising yourselves, in terms of a defence, before anything happened within your village or in its vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: The organisation boiled down to guarding water sources and power facilities. No action was taken which would have jeopardised anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but were you threatened by anything at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I do not understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in this region of Dubrovnik, including Slano, absolutely nothing was going on at the time, except that, as you put it, you had organised yourselves to guard economic facilities and other things that you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I've already said we did that. We didn't do anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you started organising yourselves in Slano, did you do this on orders that you received from the Crisis Staff in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: No. This was the Crisis Staff of Slano. I don't know anything about connections between the Crisis Staff in Slano and the Crisis Staff in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether anybody had ordered Slano, to put it that way - not to mention Dubrovnik or other towns - to start organising these units that are supposed to guard the village or town in any way? Do you know who launched this initiative? Because absolutely nothing was going on in your region at the time.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: These were not any special kind of units. These were just local people wearing civilian clothes. Their duty was to guard the water supply or the power facilities, like transmission stations and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But as you say in paragraph 4 of your statement, local crisis committees were formed in order to deal with the looming danger.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I don't know where I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you are testifying on the basis of this Rule, according to which there is no live testimony, I am speaking only on the basis of your written statement. You say, "Local crisis committees were formed." This is in the middle of paragraph 4 of your statement. "Local crisis -- to combat the impending danger, local crisis committees were formed." So it's not that I'm construing anything. I'm just asking you about what you stated in your own statement.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I was not a member of the crisis committee. I was just supposed to do what I had been ordered to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you are referring to some impending danger, something that was not in place there and then, but you were expecting some kind of danger, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't the one who decided about that. There was the Crisis Staff. I was not a member of the Crisis Staff or the local crisis committee, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, the time when you started organising these local crisis committees there was actually no danger; isn't that correct at least?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know the time when this was established, because you refer to it in your statement. You talk about impending danger, and you know that there was no danger there at the time. There was nothing going on. Is that right or is that not right, Mr. Knezic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Well, things were happening in Vukovar, and that was probably the main reason why the organisation of the crisis committee was embarked upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did this local crisis committee work in accordance with guidelines provided by the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Well, as you can see in the statement, it says that "The local crisis committee received instructions from Dubrovnik." But I was not a member of the crisis committee, so I cannot answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. But you wrote in this statement that the local crisis committee was receiving instructions from Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about this a short while ago, and you said you did not know about that and that you organised yourselves on your own and that you did not have any connections with Dubrovnik; whereas, in your statement you say that you were given instructions by Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes, as it was put here, the local crisis committee. I was just supposed to carry out what the local crisis committee had told me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you received orders from Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: The local crisis committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what kind of orders were these? What did they pertain to?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I cannot speak about that. I was not a member of the crisis committee. I can only say that I did what the crisis committee told me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what did they tell you to do, the crisis committee?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Within a given period of time, I was, for example, supposed to guard the water supply that is right above the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What kind of weapons did you have then, when you were guarding this water supply?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I specifically did not have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who had weapons?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Somebody who was in the group. Well, perhaps one hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Knezevic [as interpreted], you say that the situation worsened. And as the situation worsened, your Crisis Staff started reaching decisions on its own, at its own initiative. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that they had hunting rifles only.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And members of the Territorial Defence joined these crisis committees and they defended the villages; is that right? That is what you say.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes. But they didn't have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So all of them defended the village unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I've already said that there was a certain number of hunting rifles and that's the only thing that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Were the villages attacked and were you defending them therefore, since you say the villages were being defended? So had they been attacked before that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: They had been attacked on the 3rd and 4th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you had put it yourself, the JNA was predominant, in terms of manpower and the equipment it had; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, you managed to defend your villages.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: No, we did not defend our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But did you defend it in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I think an attempt was made to defend it, but it could not ultimately be defended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Knezic, that from the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff and the ZNG you got orders to attack JNA members whenever possible and wherever possible, those who were retreating from the area? From that area, Northern Dalmatia and ...?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I have not heard of such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have not heard of any such thing?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that as for the local population, together with them there were members of the National Guards Corps in that area and also some foreign mercenaries?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: No, I did not hear anything about that, and I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nothing?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about Slano.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 6 you say that on the 3rd of October, 1991 the Bijelo Brdo TV transmitter was destroyed and that is how war started in your area.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were there any positions of the ZNG at Bijelo Brdo and was the JNA fired at from there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I said that there were no members of the National Guards Corps in my area, and at that position, at the transmitter, the TV repeater at Bijelo Brdo, there wasn't anyone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was no one at Bijelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please: You say that the bay of Slano was shelled from sea and from the direction of Popovo Polje; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how many local people from Slano were injured or killed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: One man was killed and a few people were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did this man get killed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: By a shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, how much was the village actually shelled? So from sea and from Popovo Polje you say it was shelled.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How long did this shelling go on?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: The shelling was carried out throughout the night between the 3rd and the 4th. And every second or third shell that was fired was inflammable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was intensive shelling all night?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And one man got killed. And the population of Slano had not left their homes at that point yet and they hadn't gone to Dubrovnik yet.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: It is already on the 3rd that the inhabitants of Slano started leaving, and they were not retreating towards Dubrovnik but towards the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Knezic, tell me, is it correct that the objective of that attack was not the village of Slano or the civilian population but the positions of what you call the defence of Dubrovnik, from where fire was opened against the members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? I don't know what you're talking about now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, was the object of the attack of the JNA the positions from which fire was opened against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I don't know that anybody fired from any positions near Slano at the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And you say that the Crisis Staff recommended to the local population to leave Slano.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that one man got killed and that there were a few persons who were wounded. However, in the statement you say that there were many persons who were wounded but that you do not remember their names. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw some of the wounded, and I heard about others. I don't remember the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Slano is a small town, a village. A short while ago you said, when I think Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff mentioned during the brief summary of your statement, that this village has a population of about 500. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're a person from Slano.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You cannot remember a single name of any one of the wounded, including those that you had only heard of? You haven't heard of a single name?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: For a while - and I've already said that - I was hiding from the shells and from the attack. So then I was not able to see all of these people. Of course, some of the wounded managed to get out towards the west and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see a single wounded person?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know at least the name of that person from your village, that small village of yours?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Goran Bebura [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any other wounded persons?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I did see some wounded persons, but it was night-time, so I was not in a position to recognise everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since it was night-time, how did you know that they were wounded?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Because they were near the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you draw this conclusion that they were wounded because they were close to the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: They were being treated by a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And in paragraph 8, you say that "The defenders were at the Admiral Hotel"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: These were a few persons who, as they were fleeing, tried to put up some resistance, and then they withdrew by boats further on, across the sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: How long did they offer resistance for? How long did that last? Because you say that they offered resistance and that then they turned towards the sea and got into boats and withdrew. So how long did this resistance last?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, a very short time. Because I wasn't actually there with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, please, once they withdrew in boats, did they withdraw to Dubrovnik then?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were on their way to Ston.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see, Ston. Now, you say that you didn't manage to pull out and that you had to go into hiding amongst some rocks with your father and a neighbour; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How long were you in hiding for?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: For two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As long as two months? Well, what did you eat during that time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: My father would go around collecting food, some tins. And at that time, it was the mandarin season and oranges were ripe and some rose-hips so that was the only food we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that "We spent two months in hiding in those rocks and during that time the three of us had a rifle and three or four bullets, and from our shelter we could see the village. There was no electricity, so we would crawl out at night and take food from our houses, from our homes." That means you went home to get food from your houses. Now you tell us that you went around collecting mandarin oranges round about, which of course is something you might have done. But what you say here is that you actually went home and took food from your own house.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: As there was an electricity -- a power cut, all the freezers and refrigerators stopped working and all the food went bad, so that in some of our houses, the ones that hadn't been set fire to yet, we did nonetheless manage to find a box of biscuits, for example, or some stale bread. Whereas, all the rest of the food that was stored in the refrigerators went bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now how is it possible for you to go into the village to take food regardless of whether the food was -- what food you took when you say that the entire village was under occupation? How were you able to do that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes, the village was under an occupation. But in the evening hours those who had occupied this settlement would withdraw towards the centre of the village and some of our houses that were located up above the road were accessible to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in paragraph 9 you talk about history repeating itself, something of that kind, and you say, "Soon after the occupation of the village, the JNA and the paramilitaries began setting fire to the house and looting, and in 1667 this happened -- those same people attacked the area. The next time was in 1806 and I hope the last time was 1991," when history seems to have repeated itself. What are you talking about there, Mr. Knezic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about what I read about in my history books.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that in -- that 90 per cent of the houses in Slano were burnt down? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was the whole of Slano burnt down then? It no longer remained standing?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Just a few houses were left standing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You even claim that members of the JNA set fire to an old woman called Ana Strazicic to force her to tell them where she had hidden some money.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: They didn't set fire to her. What happened was that they lit a fire underneath her bed. She was bed ridden and sick and she lived there with her husband and they wanted to extort money from her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But later on she died a natural death. She was ill and she died of natural causes later on. Is there anybody that can corroborate what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes, her husband, Mirko Strazicic, and my father, Antun Knezic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did the woman die of natural causes?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone harm her on the occasion when you say that this fire was lit or when you say that she was set on fire?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I did not say they set her on fire. What I said was that they lit a fire underneath her bed to make her frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But did anybody harm her? Since you say that they lit a fire underneath her, she must have been hurt.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, who was there? Which of these people were there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Her husband -- her husband was there and my father was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you nonetheless say that the woman died of natural causes.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes, later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, later on. I understand. Now, you also say that they wanted to rape the wife of a fisherman but didn't actually do so.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I heard about that when I was set free, after I had been liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know they wanted to? You say they wanted to rape this man's wife but didn't, so what was all this about? What did you actually see and who actually told you that? Because you saw none of it. You just say that somebody told you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Well, I say what I heard from the wife's family members, some of her relations, and she stayed in Slano.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But nothing happened to the woman, as far as I can see from your statement.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: She wasn't raped, but her husband, who tried to defend her, was shot in his legs from a firearm and was taken for treatment to Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was wounded in Slano, but quite obviously not whilst defending his wife, because he wasn't able to defend her successfully and she wasn't raped either.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: He tried to defend her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And nothing happened to her, although he wasn't successful in his attempt to defend her. Was he perhaps not wounded on some other occasion and not in defence of his wife?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: No, he was defending his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But nothing happened to her, did it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: That means that he did succeed in defending her in some way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If that's your conclusion, then we can move on. Mr. Knezic, in paragraph 13 you mention your father, who was captured in December 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: What happened to him after that? Was he taken to Bileca too or was he released?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: He wasn't taken to Bileca, and neither was he released. He spent the entire time in Mirko Strazicic's house, in a sort of house arrest, under house arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Mirko Strazicic's house is in fact located in Slano, is it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of house arrest? Did anybody tell him he wasn't allowed to leave the house or what?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: He had to have a permit, a pass to go and take food to them, because they were elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did anybody stand guard in front of their house? Was it a sort of prison or what, or was it an ordinary house and he lived in the house of this man Strazicic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: He always had to be in the house if somebody were to come by to control and see whether he was there. And if he went out for food, he had to have a permit or pass to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How often did an inspection come by? Was there a military unit all the time, or would people come and inspect the house from time to time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I think that people came to inspect the house from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, there's no sense in me pursuing the point. Tell me now: Three days later, on the 4th of December, in fact, you were arrested, together with a man called Bozo Glumac. And you talk about that in paragraph 13. You say that you were arrested by members of the Uzice Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: While you were being arrested, you had arms on you, didn't you? You had a weapon on you. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I had an old army -- no, I apologise. An old hunting rifle belonging to my grandfather.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when you were arrested, you had a rifle on you, did you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I said I had an old hunting rifle belonging to my grandfather.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me, how come you were able to say that it was the Uzice Corps which arrested you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: The people taking me into custody, capturing me, told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you claim that you learnt about that only when you were taken to Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that was the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when they brought you to Bileca, did they tell you, "We are members of the Uzice Corps," or what? Did they introduce themselves and tell you what corps they were from? Is that what you're claiming, Mr. Knezic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, in Bileca I learnt about it being the Uzice Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who from?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I heard from the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 14, you say that in the room that you were in -- you were interviewed in, questioned in, a local arrived, a local came into the room by the name of Momcilo Tubic and he pretended he didn't recognise you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what was he doing there? Was he a member of the Uzice Corps too?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I don't know what he was doing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Or was he wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I think he was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was a local, you say, but he was wearing civilian clothes. How could he have gone to a military facility wearing civilian clothes? Why did he come there in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim that they gave you food to eat and that was the first time that you had seen bread for the past two months, the two months you spent in hiding; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that means that as soon as you were brought there, they fed you straight away.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: No. I was questioned first, interrogated first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the very next day, on the 5th of December, you and Glumac were transferred to Bileca; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And together with you, as you say, there was some officer from Trebinje; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So both Trebinje and Bileca are on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's right, isn't it, Mr. Knezic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at the time the Yugoslav People's Army, both on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as on the territory of Croatia, was the regular army, belonging to the state, so an army on its own territory? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All this is taking place in 1991; that's right, isn't it, Mr. Knezic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you are saying you were arrested by members of JNA and taken to Bileca and Trebinje. You were in Trebinje, Bileca and Slano. Now, at that time - and the period is 1991 - was the JNA the sole regular army on the territory of the former Yugoslavia or was there some other army there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I don't know about any other army, and I don't know why the JNA was supposed to attack Slano.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going into that. I really don't know about that. What I'm trying to do is to learn what you know about and what you're testifying about. So tell me, Mr. Knezevic [as interpreted], you were not a member of the Croatian National Guards Corps, were you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But at the point of your arrest, you had a weapon on you, and it was considered that you had taken part in the attacks on the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I didn't attack anybody. I didn't fire a single bullet. And I'm not a hunter either, so I don't really know how to load a rifle either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the men who captured you couldn't have known that. They came across you with a weapon and they assumed, I suppose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, the witness can't possibly answer what was in the minds of those who arrested him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I assume he can answer this question: What does he think? Why was he sent to this collection centre in Bileca? In what capacity? He was arrested bearing arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can't answer for what somebody might have thought or somebody else's reasoning. But he can be asked this: Did they -- when they arrested you, Mr. Knezic, did they tell you why they were arresting you and why they were taking you to these camps? Did they say anything to explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody explained anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Knezic. Now, upon arrival in Bileca, as you yourself say, a certain man called Ivan Tanovic introduced himself and told you he was from Uzice on the occasion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he a soldier, an officer, a man wearing a uniform, a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, is it true that he said that he was from Uzice, not that he was actually a member of the Uzice Corps that, he was from Uzice, that he was born in Uzice, that that was his native town?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes. And his nickname was Ivan of Uzice, "od Uzice."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: A military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was a soldier. He didn't have a rank of any kind, did he?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him with a rank insignia. When he came up and he broke my ribs, I wasn't able to see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means the man beat you, did he?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he beat anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I didn't see at all, because there were just the two of us in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say that over the next few days members of the JNA interrogated you and they mistreated you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did they question you about? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I can't really remember very well, but I think the interrogations were linked to the defence of the locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they ask you about a National Guards Corps unit, the number of soldiers this unit had and questions along those lines?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I said that in my village there was no National Guards Corps unit, and I think they knew that, so they didn't have to put any such questions to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what, then, did they ask you? As you are talking about an interrogation, what did they ask you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I think I've already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I won't insist. Can't you remember what they asked you about? Tell me, then: Do you remember seeing the nickname of one of those men? And you say that his name was Biga. Where is that man from?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I don't know where he's from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim that he was a JNA captain.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes, because he had such a rank insignia on his uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, you say that he was wearing an SMB uniform. Is that why you claim that he was a JNA member? And a captain by rank?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you as a member of the reserve force of the JNA have a similar uniform at home?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any uniforms at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone else have them in Slano?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I didn't see them. I think that no one had any uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, these guards who beat you, that you say mistreated you at night, were they also JNA members?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were guards in the camp in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you claim that there were guards who treated you like human beings, as you put it, treated you decently. I see that you keep checking through your statement. I do assume that you do recollect some of these things.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember very well all the mistreatment that I was subjected to for a total of 212 days in two camps. And for that reason I can't sleep well. I find it difficult to concentrate. And I am -- I am not very good at fulfilling my responsibilities. I have a wife and three children at home. I was taken to two camps for absolutely no reason, and I repeat, I spent 212 days there absolutely for no reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Knezic, please, did an officer of the JNA ever beat you or mistreat you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Mistreatment doesn't merely imply beating. Mistreatment also includes psychological mistreatment, which it is very difficult to stand. To be more specific, during my stay in two camps, I went seven times to be exchanged. We were promised that we would be exchanged in three or four days, and this was a mere lie, and it was only on the seventh occasion that at an exchange which was not an exchange, on the 2nd of July, 1992 in Cavtat, I was released - I can call it that - from the camp in Morinj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were released in Cavtat, and this was not an exchange, was it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to gather, our exchange had been prepared for the 5th of May that year, but it didn't take place and I didn't see anyone moving from Brod to the buses that we were brought there in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were released without an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the arrangement was. I just know that this was on the 212th day of my detention in two camps, without any reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am very sorry, Mr. Knezic, that this happened to you. I'm just asking you questions to establish the facts. So if no officer ever beat you and there were guards who treated you decently, can you claim that those who beat you received orders from a higher place to beat you, whether they be JNA or from someone else, or was it just arbitrary behaviour by individuals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can't say whether the men had orders unless they said something to him. Did anybody say whether they'd been ordered to beat you or not, Mr. Knezic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. But I do know that beatings were a daily occurrence, and they would wake us up at night. Again for no reason we would be beaten. And while being beaten, we had to hold our hands behind our heads and look down at the floor. So we couldn't always know who was beating us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on the 23rd of June, 1992, you were transferred to Morinj in the territory of Montenegro; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I think that's not the right date. I think it was the -- the 23rd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see, in May. And you say that in Morinj too you were beaten. Do you know who were the guards who beat you there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I said that whenever we moved around, we had to look down, look at the floor. Our hands had to be behind our heads, and none of us dared to look at who was beating us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that. But tell me, please: You do distinguish between the people who beat you and those who treated you decently. So could you at least tell us who were the people who treated you decently? Because I assume they would not prevent you from looking at them if these others who beat you would not let you look at them.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Regardless who was with us in a particular area or room, we had to look down. This was humiliating. We didn't know who was beating us. But in most cases they must have been the prison guards. I just know that especially in Morinj - I don't know his name - there was a young man who told us a little about what was happening outside, because throughout that time we were in total isolation in terms of information. We had no information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 39, you say that on the 13th of June, 1992 a certain Gligic tortured you and beat you in Morinj. He was wearing a JNA uniform, but you say he was not a member of the army. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: With regard to him, they said that he was a reservist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say, "He was wearing an SMB uniform, greyish-olive-green, but I'm sure he was not a regular member of the JNA." You go on to say that "He was much older than the regular soldiers and this was confirmed to us by the prison guards as well."

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You yourself say that you never saw a single JNA officer issuing orders to a soldier, a reservist, or a guard to beat the prisoners, is that right, but you assume that they had their permission to do that. Is that right, Mr. Knezic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I think it is logical for a soldier to carry out orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's time now for the adjournment. Mr. Milosevic, there will be ten minutes more for your cross-examination, if you require it. Mr. Knezic, could I please remind you not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution. Could you be back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Knezic, did I understand you correctly that this mistreatment that you described took place at night?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: There was mistreatment by day and by night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you never saw a single JNA officer giving orders to a soldier to mistreat people, so I -- surely you know that that is a crime, to mistreat prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I don't know how I could have been a prisoner of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is probably how they treated you, because they arrested you with a weapon on you. I'm just assuming. I'm not claiming that.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I didn't have a weapon in my hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you said you did. But that doesn't change anything regarding these explanations.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that I had a weapon on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you said you were arrested with a rifle that was your grandfather's.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. But I didn't have the weapon in my hand. It was hidden away so as not to get wet from the rain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever learn whether there were any proceedings against any person who mistreated you or anyone else, a criminal or any other kind of proceedings against such persons?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard regarding the commander of the Bileca camp, Branko Ljubisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If proceedings were instituted against the commander, I assume you must have heard that similar proceedings were instituted against other perpetrators of such impermissible acts. Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You just mentioned, according to your own knowledge - and I cannot be privy to that knowledge - you mentioned one of the camp commanders. What was the name of the other camp commander in Morinj?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I never learnt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see from what you wrote here, you mentioned that the commander of the camp in Bileca was Miodrag Nikolic, and now you mentioned a different name of the commander, saying that proceedings were instituted against him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we got there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see what the point the accused is trying to make. He's mentioned one name in his evidence. Are you putting another name to him now, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am pointing to his testimony, in which -- in his statement, in which he mentioned the name Miodrag Nikolic. I'm not saying anything other than what I find in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which paragraph is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thirty-five, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Well, Mr. Knezic, the point that's made is that you mentioned two names -- you've now mentioned two names as the commander at Bileca. Can you assist us as to how that comes about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when I got there, there was the Uzice Corps, and he was replaced -- the corps -- that corps was replaced by the Rijeka Corps. And this mentioned Branko Ljubisic is from the Rijeka Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Regarding this Ljubisic, it is known that he was called to account for what happened there. As for Nikolic, you don't know anything about him.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: While Nikolic was in command, was there mistreatment of prisoners as well?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from this one person that you heard was called to account, do you know of anyone else being prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Knezic. While you were either in Bileca or in Morinj or in both, did any representative of the Red Cross come and visit you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Yes. On several occasions, representatives of the International Red Cross did visit us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you were so badly mistreated, as you say, did you pass on that information to representatives of the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: People were afraid to tell them anything, because they were in fear and they feared further mistreatment, and it was also possible for a man to have a sandbag and then be beaten and then no traces are left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that when you spoke to representatives of the International Red Cross you had no visible traces of mistreatment on you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: A broken rib cannot be shown to anyone. It is only visible under an x-ray.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the other prisoners, did they have any traces of mistreatment? Because you say that the International Red Cross visited you several times. So surely they must have noticed traces of mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Psychological mistreatment in particular are not so clearly visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about psychological mistreatment. Of course, the very fact that one is in prison is psychological mistreatment. But I'm asking you about physical mistreatment. And due to several visits by the International Red Cross, I'm asking you whether they noticed any traces of that physical mistreatment on the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you should ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't complain to any one of them, did you, you yourself?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: We were all afraid to complain of anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So no one complained. And apart from the Red Cross, were there any physicians in either of the camps?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: Only once did I see a doctor, in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did that doctor intervene in relation to you or to someone else, and in what -- under what circumstances? Did he examine you, this doctor?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: He just brought some pills that the men needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you able, according to the rules in the camp, to ask? Could you ask to see a doctor?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of rules you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did any one of those people who were responsible for you in the camp say that there was the possibility for you to see a doctor if you needed medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I never heard of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then how did this doctor bring pills to some of the men who needed them if nobody had requested medical assistance? Did he do it just like that, or did you just see it happen?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I saw this only once. He came. He asked whether anybody needed some kind of pills. Later on he brought them, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In addition to the International Red Cross, did any other humanitarian organisation have a representative of theirs come and see you? Anybody outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I know that during the first and second visit of the International Red Cross I had been hidden. It was only during their third visit that I was registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You must bring this to a close, please. But you can ask two more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the total number of visits of this International Red Cross to Bileca and Morinj, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I think that the visits were on average once a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means during this time there had to have been at least seven visits, if it were once a month.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I said "on average," so it could have been even less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did anybody receive a visitor? Did any relatives, friends come and visit the prisoners there, anybody, any one of the prisoners who were there in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: I did not receive any visits, and I did not hear of anybody else receiving any visitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Knezic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is attached to the statement the photograph of the witness's house, I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And it was burnt. And I have only -- and attached are also some medical records, but they refer to the psychological result --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- of the detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Various psychological reports. We've seen those.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And I have only one question to clarify one matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic inquired about the hunting rifle of your grandfather. When you surrendered to the -- to the Uzice Corps, to the soldiers, did you have that hunting rifle with you and did you hand it over?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KNEZIC
utterances.text: The hunting rifle, as I said, was near the rock where I was hiding with my father and my neighbour. There was no ammunition in it. It was not used. And the soldiers who took me prisoner took it themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Knezic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There'll be a few minutes to arrange the voice distortion for the next witness. Are there any administrative matters meanwhile, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Not -- not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what I have here now, the next witness is not a protected witness. Is the list I have wrong?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if you have the witness -- the witness list I think of the 9th of September - I could be wrong about the date - but the one that I have most certainly has the next witness as a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a lady with a name and surname here. Now, let me take a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think you'll find she's protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness would like to take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Madam, in front of you is a sheet of paper. Is there your name on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You gave a statement to an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor in the year 2000. Did you have an opportunity to read and confirm this statement, with some additions, in a proceeding in front of a court officer during your stay here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would like to tender the 92 bis statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the pseudonym sheet will be 544 under seal, and the statement will be 545 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I will now read the summary. The witness is a Croatian female. She was a resident of Vukovar during the events. Beginning of July 1991, the JNA started shelling Vukovar. From the 25th of August, 1991 onwards, Vukovar was surrounded from all sides. The shelling intensified and the witness and six other civilians took shelter in the basement of a house until the 16th of September, 1991. The group ventured outside on the 16th of September and encountered 10 to 15 men, JNA reservists from Vukovar and elsewhere. These soldiers forced them back into the house. All the while, the witness could hear people screaming, crying, and a lot of shooting. From the 16th of September until the 12th of October, 1991, the witness and about ten other Croatian civilians were detained in different Serb houses, guarded by JNA reservists. They had to put a white ribbon on their arms. One of the houses was a kind of headquarters for the soldiers. During their detention, the witness and the other detainees, most of them women and children, were interrogated. While the women were only verbally abused, one of the male detainees, a friend of the witness, was physically mistreated. On the 12th of October, 1991, two soldiers took the detainees to Velepromet factory. Ten additional Croats, including children and women, were already there. Upon arrival, the witness's friend, the male civilian, was taken away for interrogation. He is missing ever since. The witness and her mother were then removed from Velepromet and again detained in different Serb houses. On the 10th of November, 1991, they were brought back to Velepromet. That same day, about 50 to 60 women, children, and elderly were transferred to the military prison in Sid --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: They were taken to a facility, a sort of movie theatre, from where most of the detainees were taken out for interrogation. The witness was interrogated throughout the night. Although the witness was not beaten herself, she heard screaming from the interrogation room next door. The witness, together with about 70 non-Serbs, mostly women, children, and old men, were driven to Becej, Vojvodina, in a bus. They were escorted by Serb soldiers. In Becej, the witness and 20 others were called out from the bus. The others were taken to Begejci camp. The witness and her group were taken to the Becej sports hall. There Sveto, a member of the Serbian state security, gave them instruction on how to behave. That night every detainee was interrogated by members of the state security of Serbia. The next morning, they were again loaded onto a bus and taken to the Sremska Mitrovica military prison. They saw a military truck bringing men from Vukovar to be detained there as well. The witness and her group were searched, their money and jewellery was taken away. After a few days, many of the detainees, among them the witness and her mother, were transferred to the Sremska Mitrovica sports hall. There they met about 1.000 civilians that had arrived at the sports hall after the fall of Vukovar. The witness's mother had to sign a form handing over her property in Vukovar to the authorities. On or around the 19th of November, 1991, a convoy was organised and the witness and her mother managed to get on the convoy that travelled through Bosnia to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, I have just one aspect to ask you about: During your detention in all these various houses in Vukovar or the facilities in Serbia, were you always guarded by armed personnel, JNA or other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And during the transfers, was that also the case? Were you also always --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In all these places, be it in the -- in Serbia or in Vukovar, could you move around freely?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: No. No, we could not move about.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you stay in all these places or any of these places on your own free will?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: I did not stay in any one of these places of my own free will.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you were transferred to Serbia, were you ever informed where you were taken and what would happen to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: No. We never knew where they were taking us and what would happen next.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever have a choice to decide where to stay and where to go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: No. There wasn't any choice. We did not have the possibility of a choice.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are the questions that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. 1164, when were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: On the 16th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that you spent two months in all these events that you've been testifying about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A short while ago you said that you did not have any choice. On the 19th of November, you were taken in a convoy through Bosnia to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that your choice, to be set free and to be safely taken to a place where you would feel safe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: The convoy in which we left was organised by the European Union, actually, with the people from Vukovar, a great many people from Vukovar, representatives of the international community also arrived, and that is how we managed to get out in this convoy, through Bosnia to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you know that the representatives of the international community were there with the agreement of the authorities of Serbia and Yugoslavia to see how people were being treated or, rather, in this particular case citizens who had been evacuated from war-affected areas, and then they were transported to safe areas.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: When we were brought from the prison in Sremska Mitrovica, there were no representatives of the international community. Still we had armed JNA soldiers around us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, this two-month episode of yours ended with your own safe departure, the safe departure of your mother, and of the other citizens who were transferred to Croatia then; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Safe, in the sense that we arrived safe and sound, but we did not belong to the convoy that came from Vukovar. We were detainees, the entire group that was there. When the convoy set out, we requested the members -- the representatives of the international community to make sure that we would leave with them, because people came on buses and everybody had their own seats on a particular bus. We were not brought -- we had not been brought with them, and people didn't know about us when they came to the sports hall in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you could have been in contact with them. So you were not concealed in any way, since you were in contact with them and you asked to be included in this convoy.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: There was a great many people there and everybody came to one hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you were transferred.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: I think everybody was. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this great many people who were evacuated from the war-affected areas stayed there for a while, where they did in Serbia, and then they were transported to Croatia on buses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. The interpreters cannot hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to put a few concrete questions to you. As far as I can see from your statement, on page 2, in paragraph 1, during the war you were serving in the Croatian army. You were assigned to a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Yes, I gave an additional statement. When I was taken prisoner, I was not a member of the Croatian army. I was working for a state agency. I was part of the services that were engaged in taking care of things that were going on in that particular building, so that would be a Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you did not belong to a military organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: No. No, not when I was taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you were not a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you became a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What qualified you for becoming a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Among the people who were there where I worked at the time, everybody was assigned a particular job. I, with a lady colleague of mine, tried to take care of everything; lists, archives, and to have it put at certain places, safe places. During those days, that's what it was, more or less. Soon afterwards, I was taken prisoner, and I did not see anybody after that. Actually, on the 13th of September it was the last time that I was at work, and then I went back and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who took you on this Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: The people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you say -- be more specific?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the full name of this Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was president?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For how long did you work on this Crisis Staff altogether?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Well, it was perhaps for about a week, and then it became impossible to move around and to come. I lived farther away from the place where I worked, so I tried to come and do the things that should have been done there, in terms of taking care of the archives and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 2, in paragraph 2, of your statement, you say that after the elections of 1990, you could feel a difference in Vukovar, that there were some tensions or something like that. Could you elaborate on that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Well, as far as I'm concerned personally, I did not see any big differences in all of this, but what it says here in my statement is that people talked about it, how the Croatian state became independent and our colleagues who worked with us were not exactly thrilled. They were ethnic Serbs and they didn't like seeing the Croatian flag even on Croatian television at the beginning and the end of the Croatian TV programme, let alone on the buildings that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was being discussed about the independence of Croatia that caused concern among the Serbs in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: I don't know whether it caused concern. They probably --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, Madam 1164, what were your own political views then in relation to these developments?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: I did not meddle in politics. I did my own job, and I thought that nothing had changed and I didn't think that attention would have to be paid to things like that, that the Croatian flag was flying on Croatian buildings in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it's not only a question of the flag, but is it true that during these first multi-party elections Slavko Dokmanovic, a Serb, was elected president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: I think those are the facts, yes. I think he was. I'm sure that that is probably common knowledge, whether he was or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you remember who won most of the votes from the parties -- of the parties at those first multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Well, all that's a question of history. I really can't say. I really don't know how the voting went at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you remember that the representatives of the League of Communists of Croatia won the largest number of votes, or the SDB -- the SKH?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has just said that she doesn't remember, and there's no point repeating it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that already in July 1991, by decree, the Assembly was dissolved, the one chosen at the elections, that its president, a Serb, Dokmanovic, was suspended and that somebody else was put in his place, Marin Vidic, a representative of the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's what happened. Now, whether that was on the -- in June or July, I really can't say, but I think those are facts.
