And it's easy to check them out, so I don't think you need me -- I really don't know, but there was Marin Vidic. Now, whether he was appointed by the deputy or what, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, his party only won 25 per cent of the votes in Vukovar, if you recall. You don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Well, as I say, I didn't really deal with statistics or politics or anything like that in Vukovar. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say on page 2, paragraph 2 - and I'm not going to delve into what you don't deal with in your statement or, rather, I'll try not to and to keep it to a bare minimum - but you say that the Croats in Vukovar, after the elections, did their best not to upset the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: When I say that and when I said that, I meant the environment I lived and worked in. And whenever there were any comments - you're going to refer to the flags again - now, I don't know when the flag began to appear, whether automatically on television or in the papers, but I and the people around me, we didn't actually react to any of this and we never -- with our colleagues, we never discussed this with our colleagues. That wasn't up to us. It wasn't our place to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Madam 1144 [as interpreted], I'm quite sure you didn't involve yourself in any of this, and I'm not trying to imply that you meddled in it, but have you heard of Tomislav Mercep?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he was the commander, was he, of those forces, the Croatian National Guards Corps, those forces that were set up in Vukovar at the time before any conflicts broke out at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: When you say "any kind of conflicts," what period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Until the conflict broke out, in fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Well, I have heard of Mercep, and I do know that for a time he worked in that secretariat or whatever it was. But from the founding of - what did you call them - the Guards or whatever, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about those sorts of activities and the persecution of the Serb ethnic group in Vukovar, the killings, the dismissals from work posts, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Where I lived and worked in my environment, none of that happened. There was none of that where I lived and worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, did you hear what happened in the different villages around Vukovar and how individuals fared, the crimes that were committed, the casualties and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that you're asking me that, let me say again that when people did start talking about what had happened somewhere, the people around us, as a general rule we didn't react to any of those stories and things that were being said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that already at the end of 1990 a man called Zeljko Ostojic testified about this and later on, probably due to his testimony, was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: No, I never heard of the name. Which testimony? Where? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was killed just half an hour after the Spegelj film was shown.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And his testimony was on that film.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: I've never heard of him, the name or the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you ever hear of anything about any decisions about ethnic cleansing of the Vukovar municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge of the visits of Vladimir Seks [phoen] and Ivan Vekic and Branimir Glavas to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: No. As I say, I'm not a political person. I've never dealt in politics, had anything to do with politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you didn't have anything to do with politics, do you know any cases in which Serbs were replaced from different posts in Vukovar and dismissed from their jobs except for this man who was mayor, president of the municipality, Mr. Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: I don't remember that until the 16th of September, when I was captured, that there were any cases of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Zdravko Egic [phoen], the director general of the Borovo company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you know nobody from the Borovo concern?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about Mirko Bejanovic, the director of Buca [phoen], and Marko Sejgl [phoen], the director of Transport, that company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: No. And I don't know anything about Borovo or who occupied what post or anything about the factory really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But do you at least know that Marin Vidic, Bili, who was a deputy of the Croatian government replaced the head of the Vukovar hospital, Dr. Rade Popovic even, and replaced him by a Dr. Vesna Bosanac? Do you remember that event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: I remember that Vesna Bosanac did begin -- become the director. Now, who replaced whom, I really can't say. And when that took place, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about these replacements and dismissals in the social insurance company, the Secretariat of the Defence of the municipality and things of that kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're wasting time here. The witness doesn't know anything about this. There's no point just going all over it time and time again with all your lists of names. Pointless, Mr. Milosevic. Why don't you move on to something else. Move on to some of her evidence about how she was arrested and detained and that kind of thing. She can deal with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I assume that it is my right to ask the witness about the events in Vukovar, because the witness was there. She's an educated woman. So I assume that she is informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's pointless asking her about things she knows nothing about, all these alleged grievances which you have. No point rehearsing them with her. You can call your own evidence about it if you want.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as you see, she does know about some of these and not about others. So I can't know in advance what the witness knows about and the things she doesn't know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. Let me ask you this, madam: Did you know about the mining of facilities owned by Serbs, that they were blown up at that time in Vukovar, that is to say, before any conflict actually broke out? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: As to what you are -- just like the questions you asked beforehand, all I know about that event and those events was what the media wrote about. I don't have any direct knowledge of these events or indirect knowledge or neither do I know anything concrete about any of these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But as you're talking about the media, did you see about the takeover by force of Radio Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: I don't think that it was taken over by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A different director was appointed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: No. Everything I'm saying is to the best of my recollections. Now, whether there was any forceful takeover -- forcible takeover, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you don't know anything about that. Now, do you know anything about the blockade of JNA facilities in Vukovar, for example, the blockade of the barracks in Vukovar, to be more specific?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: As far as I know, the barracks were not blocked until the time that I was taken into custody. So I didn't hear about the blockade of the barracks at all, that it had actually been blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How come you didn't -- well, if you haven't heard anything about that, then I won't ask you about that any more. Now, was any -- were any of your family members members of any political party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Or perhaps of some military formation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just let me consult my notes and take a moment, please. I should like to ask you, Madam 1164, for your comments on this. I'm not quite clear on paragraph 6 of your statement it says, "Around the 4th of September, I asked soldiers from our -- our soldiers to come to my place and take grenades that my father had in our house. I knew that I would never use them. Our soldiers always told us that everything was under control, that nothing would happen, and that we shouldn't worry."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: What it says in my statement -- when I say "our soldiers," I mean people who were civilians who were there, the men there, the males around the house who at that time, towards the end of August and beginning of September, took care of the rest of the civilians in the area. That meant that, for example, they would -- there was a lot of shelling, terrible shelling, so they collected some sand and put the sand up in sandbags around the windows. Potatoes were being handed out to everybody there in the local commune. So that's what I said -- meant when I said "soldiers," the people who were there. They weren't actually people wearing uniforms of any kind. They were all our neighbour, people who lived around that place. They were all Croats by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what you want to say. But as you are testifying on the basis of your statement, then I saw you talking about soldiers. Now, what other weapons were there in your house except for these grenades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Nothing, nothing. No other weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did your father have these grenades in the house in the first place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: I don't know. Had I known about them, I would probably have told him that we didn't need that. I just happened to come across them. When I found them, I handed them over, because my mother and I were alone in the house, and I tried to get rid of them as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did he come to possess these grenades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. You just came across them, found them, and then asked that they be got rid of.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: May I remind both the witness and the accused not to speak at the same time, please. Madam C-1164, could you watch the accused's microphone, and when the light goes out, answer, but not before. In that way we will then maintain the protection. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago, during the brief examination-in-chief, that you were there when the shelling started, that you were in the basement, actually, in the cellar; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when was that exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: The shelling --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When were you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Well, before we were taken prisoner, we were in the basement practically every day when there was shelling going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us a date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Up until the 16th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say in your statement on page 3, paragraph 3, that you saw people who were reservists of the JNA -- I think Mrs. Uertz-Retzlaff was quoting you, or you said that they were reservists who were locals, the local inhabitants that you saw there. Is that right? Once you left the basement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Not all of them, but some of them, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So as you knew them, you concluded that they were the locals; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say -- you said that they looked frightening because they had chains with Orthodox crosses on them. Is that what you said? And I'm quoting from your statement, paragraph 8, if you count the last paragraph on page 3 of your statement. You say that "I knew at least five of them by sight. I went to school with them. They were from the village of Negoslavci. All these men were reservists of the JNA before the war started in Croatia. The group was really scary to look at. They were carrying chains with Orthodox crosses, they were dirty, had long beards," and so on. Tell me, please, what is the difference between an Orthodox cross and a Catholic cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: I was just waiting for the interpretation. Well, the difference is in the shape. They look different. An Orthodox cross looks different from a Catholic cross. And one of the men who came and whom I recognised had this big Orthodox cross, and he was my neighbour, a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But that's not what I meant by my question. What I want to know is this: Apart from the difference in the words "cross" - "kriz" in Croatian and "krst" in Serbian - where is the Orthodox cross different from the Catholic cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Well, it looks different in shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Witness. Well, one lives and learns throughout life. As far as I can see, you were detained in the house of a certain Tomasevic in Vukovar. Is that right? Is it true that in the yard of Tomasevic's house a Kalashnikov was found that had been buried there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Yes. My friend, he was taken out of the basement and he was told to dig, and he unearthed a Kalashnikov buried next to the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On Saturday, the 12th of September, 1991 a certain Bozidar Bauk was taken away. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Yes. Not on the 12th of September but on the 12th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. Then I am mistaken. And what happened to this Bauk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Nothing is known of him. There's no trace of him to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from this Bauk who you say was taken away and of whom nothing is known, I do not see from your statement that during your detention anything happened along the lines of physical torture or mistreatment or anything like that during your detention.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: No physical torture, but psychological, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course the very fact that you had to stay in that house was a kind of torture, but did anyone insult you, threaten you? What did this psychological torture consist of, apart from the fact, which of course I am not denying, that if somebody is keeping you in detention, that that is a form of torture as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: We were taken for interrogation several times, so that was real torture. That did take place. Constant questioning whenever they wanted, they would take us along the street with our hands behind our backs and our heads bowed, to some houses where we were questioned every time by someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your hands were tied?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: No, mine were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they took you to some houses to question you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who questioned you? Were they civilians or soldiers or reservists? Could you perhaps be a little more specific in describing those who questioned you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: They were always military persons. There was never a civilian at the other end of the table. They were always people wearing olive-grey military uniforms of different age groups who were questioning us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that they wore these olive-grey uniforms and were of different ages, does that mean that they were local reservists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: Yes, I assume. So I didn't know them. It could have been an active-duty officer of the then-JNA. I didn't know them. I didn't know the people who were questioning me, but they were always people in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 5, second paragraph you say that Serb soldiers even informed your mother about you, where you were, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164
utterances.text: That was when they took me for questioning. It lasted so long, and then my mother asked to be told where she was. This was in the prison in Sid and she came up to one of the soldiers and asked him to inquire what had happened to me, because she was terrified because they had taken Bozidar and now they had taken me and she thought that I wouldn't come back. So I don't know whether he checked or not, but anyway she plucked up courage and strength to come and to beg him to find out where I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must adjourn now. It is the time. Witness C-1164, we have to adjourn now. Could you be back tomorrow, please, at 9.00 to conclude your evidence. Could you remember, please, also not to speak to anybody about it until it's over. Mr. Milosevic, you've got half an hour more, if you require it, for this witness. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
